items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: these guys are the guys that were with Paul Chambers throughout Miles’s, you know, reign at the time.

ctx.x: Yeah. I wonder if you had had a recording experience where for whatever reason you weren’t quite comfortable with the leader’s concept musically, spiritually or otherwise, that you didn’t really feel that you fit in with where this music, what this music was trying to accomplish.

Well no and yes. I, as mentioned before, my intent has always been to express regardless. It’s just like getting, you know, something from myself that would better myself as having engaged myself in something, again, like Roy Haynes said, “Music is my therapy.” And so, but there have been moments where I have struggled because of the inability to fashion certain qualities of intent on the instrument. For instance, driving back to New York from Boston the other day, I teach there on Mondays and I drive back on…

Cobb and Wynton Kelly because of my inspiration — I’m sounding almost just like Paul. But when it came to soloing I wasn’t really too comfortable with that because I was still working on various techniques to improve even upon what Paul was doing. See when, in the Army, I decided to add this finger to my pizzicato adventures. You know? Usually you can play with one finger, for better technique two fingers, for me I decided to use a third. And when in the Army, during all that practice, I worked on that. So when I…

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: But apparently I did something right because I found myself on the gig for next week in Buffalo, New York. And the moment I hit the stage Miles put me through the heat man

ctx.x: No. I didn’t record with Miles Davis, but I had an episode with Miles Davis. Herbie Hancock called me — well what’s that, my first recording we discussed before, with Grachan Moncur featuring Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams. This is how I met Herbie and those guys. And so apparently I was rather impressive with my dynamic. Herbie called me and says, “Miles would like you to do a performance with him.” So I said, “Yeah, okay.” And by now, I mean that was like a couple of years later. By now I’m…

mean playing with Jack and Keith were just all I was about. But on 77th Street on the third floor of Miles’ brownstone we had gone through all the tunes, the music was like that — right? And no Miles Davis. Right? So at the conclusion of the rehearsal, the last tune in the Key of C there was Herbie and Wayne were at the piano discussing the voicing of a G something chord, a G 7 chord. And they couldn’t find it. All of a sudden burst through the door was Miles Davis. He went over to the piano and he said…
Well he was a boxer, wasn’t he?
